newsitem.title: INDIA: Death toll in India dengue fever outbreak hits 156.
newsitem.headline: Death toll in India dengue fever outbreak hits 156.

text.p: The death toll in an outbreak of dengue fever in the Indian capital rose to 156 on Tuesday, but officials said the rate of fatalities appeared to be slowing.

"Even though the number of people reporting sick of dengue fever is quite high, the number of deaths is going down due to their timely arrival (for treatment)," Vinod Jain, a senior Delhi health official, told Reuters.
Hospitals have been instructed not to turn away any patient reporting sick with dengue fever, he added.
Dengue, a mosquito-borne disease which is also called breakbone fever, erupted in New Delhi in the last week of August during annual monsoon rains.
With 11 more deaths reported overnight, at least 156 persons had died in the city and 3,290 were admitted to hospitals with dengue, Jain said.
Non-governmental organisations say the actual figures could be much higher as the official death toll does not include casualties in private hospitals.
"What we are seeing is only the tip ot the iceberg as the data available is coming from very limited places," said Pramesh Bhatnagar of the Voluntary Health Association of India.

On Monday, Delhi Lieutenant-Governor P.K. Dave asked the army to open its hospitals to patients with dengue fever and to deploy units to spray areas of the capital where mosquitoes that carry the disease breed, an aide to Dave said.

Accompanied by high fever, headaches and pain in muscles and joints, dengue normally runs its course in six to seven days. But a haemorrhagic form of dengue that can lead to internal bleeding and death has spread in the crowded capital.
Health officials said the epidemic had taken the largest toll of lives in 20 years in any single outbreak in the city.
"It is more of a system failure," Bhatnagar said. "We do not have an organised set-up that can take care of emergencies and contingencies like this one," he added.
The World Health Organisation said in a statement on Monday that more than 2.5 million people were at risk of dengue fever infection in more than 100 countries worldwide.
